meta.title: Technology Leadership & Enterprise AI — Jacek Janczura
meta.description: What I have led and owned: a bootstrapped enterprise AI company at €1M+ annual revenue, engineering grown from 0 to 10, ISO 27001 and SOC 2 in about three months, and production AI for a pension administrator, an industrial procurement organisation and a development bank.

hero.title: From customer boardroom to production code.
hero.sub: I co-founded Jaden Data and led it as CTO to €1M+ annual revenue with no external capital, grew engineering from 0 to 10, and owned AI delivery for APG, Bosch, KfW Bank and Boehringer Ingelheim — with earlier real-time systems work for ING through SAS Institute. I work from executive discovery and technical pre-sales through architecture, code, production rollout and handover, and I still write the code.

pillars.title: Four things a technology leader is accountable for
pillars.lede: Each one with the strongest single piece of evidence I have, and the case behind it.

items.title: Customer & commercial
items.body: Discovery, executive workshops, technical pre-sales, architecture and security reviews, scoping and business cases. I am in the room when a buyer decides whether the technology can be trusted.
items.proof: Four procurement workflows at a global automotive group taken from a scoped use case to production, with the alignment cadence raised from bi-weekly to weekly and split into parallel sub-groups so no single dependency stalled delivery.

items.title: Architecture & delivery
items.body: AI systems, enterprise integration, evaluation, observability, reliability, and the rollout into somebody else's production environment.
items.proof: A member-facing pension assistant prototyped in a day from platform components and delivered as an on-premises MVP in twelve sprints under Dutch financial regulation; a Dutch ministry highlighted it as one of the best examples of impactful AI integration.

items.title: Team & operating model
items.body: Hiring, mentoring, delivery standards, roadmap, technical budget, escalation and handover.
items.proof: Engineering grown from 0 to 10 inside a bootstrapped €1M+ company, with code-review standards and CI/CD quality gates in place before the team grew, and ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type 2 delivered in about three months without freezing the roadmap.

items.title: Reuse & product feedback
items.body: Every deployment leaves something behind — an integration, an evaluation harness, a playbook, a change to the product — so the next one starts further along than the last.
items.proof: One specification template and one evaluation template carried a seven-part proof-of-concept portfolio at a German development bank; the process patterns, the cited-retrieval design and the Testbed evaluation framework were reused across later deployments.

built.title: Nobody handed me a platform, a team or a client list

items.title: A company
items.body: Jaden Data was bootstrapped: no external capital, every platform investment paid for by client delivery. It passed €1M in annual revenue while I was its CTO.

items.title: A product
items.body: entAIngine grew out of client workflows instead of a speculative roadmap — one multi-tenant, provider-independent platform serving 50+ organisations at 99.9% uptime, rather than a bespoke stack per client.

items.title: A team
items.body: Engineering went from my own commits to ten people across frontend, backend and AI workstreams, with structured code review, pair programming and internal knowledge sharing.

items.title: A delivery process
items.body: Code-review standards, CI/CD quality gates and testing requirements were in place before the headcount arrived, so production quality never depended on one person being awake.

items.title: Client relationships
items.body: Technical pre-sales, project kick-offs, weekly stakeholder cadences and executive reporting were mine to run, for clients in procurement, pensions, development finance and pharma.

items.title: A security posture
items.body: ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type 2 ran as an engineering programme — controls, evidence collection and process changes alongside delivery — and were certified in about three months.

items.title: Reusable foundations
items.body: The Testbed evaluation framework, Prompt Wizard and the reusable process components came out of repeated client needs; those components are what turned a one-day prototype into a product.

principles.title: Four rules I do not bend

items.title: Understand the workflow and its baseline before choosing technology
items.body: Model choice is the last decision, not the first. What does this work cost today, who does it, where does it break, and what would make the result trustworthy to the person who signs it off?
items.example: At a German development bank every proof of concept started from one specification template — background, problem, objective, scope, methodology, success metrics, dependencies — so seven very different workflows could be compared on the same terms.

items.title: Ship the smallest real production loop
items.body: A demo proves nothing about real data, real integrations and real governance. I build the thinnest end-to-end path a real user can run, then widen it.
items.example: APG's assistant was a working prototype in one day from platform components; the twelve sprints that followed went into integration, user validation and the on-premises environment where it had to live.

items.title: Treat evaluation, security and observability as product capabilities
items.body: If a system cannot be measured, audited and watched, it is not finished. Those parts belong in the architecture from the start, not after the pilot goes well.
items.example: Testbed made AI processes and retrieval pipelines testable with deterministic cases; ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type 2 were delivered as an engineering programme in about three months while client delivery continued.

items.title: Leave a stronger team and a system somebody else can run
items.body: The measure of the work is what still functions after I stop attending the standup: standards, written decisions, and people who make the calls.
items.example: The code-review rules, CI/CD quality gates and testing requirements outlasted my time as CTO, and the reusable components and evaluation templates are what make each new deployment cheaper than the last.

handsOn.title: I did not stop writing code when I started leading

items.title: Taufolio
items.body: A current build of my own: an AI equity-research system that turns SEC filings, earnings-call transcripts and market data into cited reports. Parallel multi-agent drafting with reconciliation and citation anchoring, so every material claim links back to the source document it came from.

items.title: RP-Matcher decisions
items.body: For an emergency-lighting manufacturer I engineered the features, benchmarked five model families with hyperparameter search, and chose the tuned random forest, which reaches 78.4% top-1 accuracy on the current corpus — then wrote down what more labelled pairs would buy, instead of reaching for a deep model the dataset could not support.

items.title: Code and tooling in the open
items.body: Repositories, experiments and the tooling I use day to day are on GitHub.

items.title: Talks and publications
items.body: Conference talks on blockchain research and applications, and peer-reviewed publications on decentralised compensation of digital content, trusted inter-organisational data processing and static vulnerability analysis.
